rule: Total paid equals interest plus principal (plus fees on a lender statement)
why it matters: A payment that doesn't add up was typed or read wrong. Every later balance inherits the error.

rule: Interest equals the balance owed before the payment times the annual rate divided by 12, rounded to the cent
why it matters: This is how a fixed-rate monthly loan is worked out. Lenders that charge by the day differ by a few cents or dollars; then the lender's statement wins.

rule: Balance after equals the balance before minus the principal in this payment
why it matters: A broken chain means a payment's principal and the balance were copied from different places.

rule: Payment numbers run 1 to N with no gaps and dates go forward
why it matters: A skipped number is usually a payment left out of the file.

rule: The last payment leaves 0.00 owing and the principal adds up to the amount borrowed
why it matters: A schedule that doesn't clear the loan was built from the wrong rate or term.

rule: Every entry (same date and memo) has debits equal to credits and no line has both
why it matters: An entry that doesn't balance can't be posted. A line with both columns filled is ambiguous.

rule: The loan payable balance in the books on each statement date equals the principal balance the lender prints
why it matters: This is the loan's reconciliation. The checker names the usual cause when the difference matches a pattern.

rule: When the lender charged interest some interest was booked to Interest expense
why it matters: No interest at all means whole payments went to the loan or to an expense account.

rule: Amounts are plain numbers with two decimals: no dollar sign and no thousands comma
why it matters: Formatted amounts break sums and imports.
